Yes. In fact, the asymptotic supremum is exactly 1+o(1). The upper bound follows from a random divisibility-chain argument; the quoted examples with \Omega(n)=k show the constant 1 is sharp.

Let \Omega(n) denote the number of prime factors of n, counted with multiplicity, and write p^{\alpha}\parallel n when p^{\alpha}\mid n but p^{\alpha+1}\nmid n.

The random chain

For every prime p, let Y_{p} be independent with exponential tail

\mathbb{P}(Y_{p}\ge t)=p^{-t}\qquad(t\ge0).

Equivalently, Y_{p} is exponential with rate \log p. For t>1, define

N(t):=\prod_{p}p^{\lfloor Y_{p}/t\rfloor}.

This is almost surely a finite integer for every t>1, because

\sum_{p}\mathbb{P}(Y_{p}\ge t)=\sum_{p}p^{-t}<\infty.

Also, if t_{1}>t_{2}>1, then

\lfloor Y_{p}/t_{1}\rfloor\le\lfloor Y_{p}/t_{2}\rfloor

for every prime p, so

N(t_{1})\mid N(t_{2}).

Thus, as t decreases from \infty to 1, the values N(t) form a random divisibility chain.

For an integer n\ge2, define

H_{n}:=\{\exists\,t>1:N(t)=n\},

and let

h(n):=\mathbb{P}(H_{n}).

If A is primitive, then the events \{H_{a}:a\in A\} are pairwise disjoint: if a single chain hits both a and b, then one of a,b divides the other. Hence, for every primitive set A,

\sum_{a\in A}h(a)\le1.

So it remains to show that, uniformly for large n,

h(n)\ge(1-o(1))\frac{1}{n\log n}.

Exact hitting probability

Let

n=\prod_{p^{\alpha}\parallel n}p^{\alpha}.

The chain hits n when, for some t>1, the required prime-power thresholds have appeared but no forbidden threshold has appeared. A direct calculation gives

h(n)=\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{n^{-t}}{\zeta(t)}\left(\sum_{p^{\alpha}\parallel n}\frac{\alpha\log p}{1-p^{-t}}\right)\,dt.

Here is the derivation. Suppose the last required threshold is the \alpha-th threshold of a prime p^{\alpha}\parallel n, occurring at parameter t. Then Y_{p}=\alpha t, with density

\alpha\log p\cdot p^{-\alpha t}\,dt.

For every other q^{\beta}\parallel n, we need

\beta t<Y_{q}<(\beta+1)t,

which has probability

q^{-\beta t}(1-q^{-t}).

For every prime r\nmid n, we need Y_{r}<t, which has probability 1-r^{-t}. Multiplying and summing over the possible final primes gives

\begin{aligned}h(n) & =\sum_{p^{\alpha}\parallel n}\int_{1}^{\infty}\alpha\log p\cdot p^{-\alpha t}\prod_{\begin{matrix}q^{\beta}\parallel n \\ q\ne p\end{matrix}}q^{-\beta t}(1-q^{-t})\prod_{r\nmid n}(1-r^{-t})\,dt \\  & =\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{n^{-t}}{\zeta(t)}\left(\sum_{p^{\alpha}\parallel n}\frac{\alpha\log p}{1-p^{-t}}\right)\,dt.\end{aligned}

Now observe that for t>1,

\sum_{p^{\alpha}\parallel n}\frac{\alpha\log p}{1-p^{-t}}\ge\sum_{p^{\alpha}\parallel n}\alpha\log p=\log n.

Therefore

h(n)\ge(\log n)\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{n^{-t}}{\zeta(t)}\,dt.

Let L=\log n. Restricting the integral to 1<t<1+\delta, with \delta>0, and writing t=1+\sigma, we get

h(n)\ge Ln^{-1}\int_{0}^{\delta}\frac{e^{-L\sigma}}{\zeta(1+\sigma)}\,d\sigma.

Since

\zeta(1+\sigma)=\frac{1}{\sigma}+O(1)\qquad(\sigma\downarrow0),

we have, uniformly for 0<\sigma\le\delta,

\frac{1}{\zeta(1+\sigma)}\ge(1-\eta(\delta))\sigma,

where \eta(\delta)\to0 as \delta\to0. Hence

\begin{aligned}h(n) & \ge(1-\eta(\delta))Ln^{-1}\int_{0}^{\delta}e^{-L\sigma}\sigma\,d\sigma \\  & =(1-\eta(\delta))\frac{1}{nL}\left(1-e^{-\delta L}(1+\delta L)\right).\end{aligned}

Choose, for example,

\delta=\delta_{x}:=(\log x)^{-1/2}.

Then for every n\ge x, L=\log n\ge\log x, so

e^{-\delta_{x}L}(1+\delta_{x}L)\le e^{-\sqrt{\log x}}(1+\sqrt{\log x})=o(1),

and also \eta(\delta_{x})=o(1). Thus, uniformly for all n\ge x,

h(n)\ge(1-o(1))\frac{1}{n\log n}.

Applying the chain to a primitive set

Let A\subset[x,\infty) be primitive. For every finite B\subset A, the disjointness of the hitting events gives

\sum_{b\in B}h(b)\le1.

Using the uniform lower bound for h(b), we obtain

(1-o(1))\sum_{b\in B}\frac{1}{b\log b}\le\sum_{b\in B}h(b)\le1.

Therefore

\sum_{b\in B}\frac{1}{b\log b}\le1+o(1),

with the o(1) depending only on x, not on B or A. Taking the supremum over finite B\subset A gives

\sum_{a\in A}\frac{1}{a\log a}\le1+o(1).

So the proposed assertion is true.

Moreover, the constant 1 is best possible: for A_{k}=\{n:\Omega(n)=k\}, one has A_{k}\subset[2^{k},\infty), A_{k} is primitive, and your quoted asymptotic gives

\sum_{\Omega(n)=k}\frac{1}{n\log n}=1-(c+o(1))k^{2}2^{-k}.

Thus the asymptotic upper bound 1+o(1) cannot be replaced by anything below 1.
